sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Continuous flow language models offer a path to parallel generation with tools for control and acceleration unavailable to discrete diffusion, yet effective techniques for building them at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. We present Lafa (Large flow language model), a fast, high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in a data-efficient manner. Lafa is a blockwise flow model with causal attention on the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. This design enables efficient training by adapting pretrained autoregressive (AR) models and fast inference via prefix caching and blockwise parallel decoding. We train Lafa at 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, more efficient than previous diffusion models, and evaluate it on instruction following, reasoning, and coding, where the learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and can be distilled into flow maps for one- and few-step generation. Notably, flow training preserves or even improves pretrained AR capabilities via a multi-token prediction effect, which we leverage in a self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively within a single model. This yields 2.54x the throughput of an AR model at comparable quality, outperforming multi-token prediction and discrete diffusion methods. Our findings show that continuous flows can serve as a scalable foundation for language modeling.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Todays large language models are predominantly trained as autoregressive (AR) models that predict the next token from the preceding text [13]. The parallelism of the transformer architecture and teacher forcing [4, 5] allows these models to be trained efficiently at the scale of billions of parameters and trillions of data tokens. However, their generation is inherently sequential, producing one token per forward pass, which makes inference latency bottleneck. To accelerate inference, prior work has explored approaches to parallel generation, namely multi-token prediction (MTP) [68], discrete diffusion models [911], and continuous flow language models [1214]. Distinguished from the other approaches, flow language models perform parallel generation by integrating continuous flow from noise to token representations [12]. By operating in continuous space, they can leverage powerful techniques developed for controllable and accelerated generation of images and video, many of which are unavailable to discrete methods [13, 14]. Yet, existing flow language models have been demonstrated at small scales and on simple tasks [1317], and 1 Figure 1: Large flow language models. Lafa 7B attains 2.022.54 the throughput of an AR model at matched or better quality, outperforming existing MTP and diffusion-based approaches. Figure 2: Overview. (Top) Lafa learns block denoiser that also performs AR prediction on the prefix. (Bottom) Lafa supports flow decoding, which can be further distilled into flow map for one-step generation. Together, AR and flow support self-speculative decoding, which accepts flow-based drafts from left to right via AR verification. prior attempt of scaling has identified challenges in training inefficiency [18]. Together, effective techniques for building performant flow language models at the billion-parameter scale remain less established. In this paper, we present Lafa (Large low language model), fast and high-performing flow language model scaled to 8B parameters in data-efficient manner. Motivated by the left-to-right directionality of text [19], we design Lafa as blockwise flow model, with causal attention on the prefix, and bidirectional but left-to-right-biased asynchronous flow within each block. This brings its architecture and inductive bias close to AR models, enabling efficient training by adapting pretrained models. Further, this allows fast inference via prefix caching and parallel flow decoding, which can be further distilled into flow maps for oneand few-step generation. We train Lafa with blockwise denoising for the flow, along with AR prediction on the prefix, and find that flow training preserves or even enhances pretrained AR capabilities through multi-token prediction effect. We leverage this in self-speculative decoding scheme that verifies flow-based drafts autoregressively. With these techniques, we train Lafa across 0.5B, 7B, and 8B scales with fewer than 30B tokens, cheaper than comparable adaptation of discrete diffusion models that use up to 500B tokens [20, 21]. Across benchmarks spanning instruction following, reasoning, and coding, Lafa attains qualityspeed frontier that surpasses similarly sized AR, MTP, and discrete diffusion language models, as shown in Figure 1. An overview of the approach is in Figure 2. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce Lafa, large flow language model that learns blockwise asynchronous flow, enabling efficient training by adapting pretrained AR models and fast inference through prefix caching and parallel flows. We identify key design choices for scalability, including the architecture and asynchronous flow formulation, training and flow map distillation objectives, and inference schemes including self-speculative decoding. We scale Lafa to 78B parameters with <30B tokens and show that its learned flow matches or surpasses the quality of AR and is distillable into flow maps, and its learning improves pretrained AR capabilities. By jointly leveraging the flow and AR capabilities for self-speculative decoding, Lafa attains 2.54 the throughput of strong AR baseline at matched quality, outperforming existing parallel generation methods. Our findings show that continuous flows offer practical, scalable foundation for parallel language modeling.

sections.content: In this section, we introduce Lafa, class of scalable and high-performing large flow language models. We first formulate blockwise asynchronous flows, then describe the architecture, training, and inference procedures. See Appendix for theoretical results and Appendix for algorithmic details.

sections.title: 2.2 Learning the flow from an autoregressive model
sections.content: As our formulation keeps causal structure, we learn the blockwise flow by adapting pretrained AR model into block denoiser. The challenge is parallel denoising of continuous, noisy embeddings while retaining AR prediction and prefix caching. Our adaptation combines tokenwise time conditioning, block-bidirectional attention, and constrained updates to pretrained embeddings with joint AR and denoising training. Tokenwise time conditioning. We feed the embedded prefix followed by the noisy block x, and condition each position on its corruption level through adaptive layer normalization (adaLN) [31]. Prefix positions always receive time 1, indicating the absence of noise, while each block position [B] receives its tokenwise time τ i(t). This lets single forward pass handle both the clean prefix and asynchronous denoising within the block. We initialize adaLN to the identity, so that adding time conditioning initially leaves the pretrained computation unchanged. We denote the resulting model by ft(x; c). Block-bidirectional attention. We make attention bidirectional within the noisy block, allowing partially denoised later tokens to inform earlier ones (Figure 3). Block positions also attend to the entire clean prefix, whose attention remains causal and excludes the noisy block [32, 33]. Together with conditioning prefix positions on time 1, this makes their keys and values independent of the block state (x, t), allowing reuse across denoising steps and subsequent blocks. The prefix outputs retain their AR role: ft(x; c)i predicts ci+1 for < , and the first block token y1 for = . We write these block-independent predictions as (c)i and use them to verify the denoisers drafts in self-speculative decoding (Section 2.3). sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: In our experiments, we evaluate whether Lafa learns flows that reach AR quality through data-efficient adaptation, and whether flow map distillation improves few-step generation (Section 3.1). We then examine how flow training affects AR accuracy (Section 3.2) and use the retained AR predictor for self-speculative decoding, measuring both parallelism and wall-clock throughput (Section 3.3). Finally, we ablate the main training and inference choices (Section 3.4). Evaluation details are in Appendix C. Models and data. We build Lafa at 0.5B and 7B by adapting the corresponding Qwen2.5 Instruct checkpoints [42] as described in Section 2. At 8B, we use Qwen3 8B Base [43], as further training of its heavily post-trained Instruct counterpart degraded performance in our experiments. We train all models on Dolci-Instruct-SFT [44] for 515 epochs (927B tokens), using at least 18 fewer training tokens than the reported budgets of Dream, LLaDA, and Efficient-DLM at comparable scales [20, 21, 45]. Benchmarks. We evaluate on six benchmarks spanning instruction following, reasoning, and code generation: IFEval (0-shot) [49], BBH (3-shot) [50], MMLU-Pro (0-shot) [51], GPQA (0-shot) [52], GSM8K (0-shot) [53], and HumanEval (0-shot) [54]. These downstream tasks assess generation quality without relying on generative perplexity, whose limitations are documented by Franca and Tong [55]. All methods are evaluated with lm-evaluation-harness [56] using each benchmarks default prompts. We report prompt-level strict accuracy for IFEval, pass@1 for HumanEval, and accuracy for the remaining tasks. Generation is capped at 1024 tokens per sample, except 512 for GSM8K and 640 for HumanEval. We report six-benchmark macro-averages for single-token accuracy and self-speculative accuracy and TPF (Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 7). For flow and flow map decoding, throughput, and ablations, we average over IFEval, GSM8K, and HumanEval, covering instruction following, math, and coding, considering their more costly evaluations.

sections.title: 3.2 Autoregressive decoding
sections.content: We next examine how joint flow training affects the retained AR capability (Section 2.2), evaluating Lafa and baselines under single-token decoding. As shown in Table 1, Lafa improves average accuracy over matched AR SFT across all three model scales (per-benchmark results in Appendix C.1). It also outperforms the matched multi-token and block-parallel baselines on average at 0.5B and 7B. At 8B, Lafa achieves similar accuracy to Efficient-DLM evaluated with single-token unmasking, while using at least 18 fewer training tokens. These results show that learning the flow can also improve AR prediction, consistent with the benefits of multi-token training [6, 8, 34]. We therefore use this retained AR predictor to verify flow-based drafts for self-speculative decoding (Section 3.3).

sections.title: 3.3 Self-speculative decoding
sections.content: We now evaluate self-speculative decoding, which verifies one-step flow drafts with the retained AR predictor (Section 2.3). We measure both parallelism, in tokens committed per forward pass (TPF), and end-to-end wall-clock throughput. Each block size uses its corresponding trained checkpoint, and self-speculation preserves that checkpoints greedy AR output. 8 Parallelism. Figure 7 and Table 2 report accuracy and TPF averaged over all six benchmarks (protocols detailed in Appendix C.1). At 0.5B, Lafa with block size eight achieves about twice the TPF of DeepSeek-MTP, MARS, and PTP while attaining higher average accuracy. At 7B, increasing the block size from four to sixteen nearly doubles TPF while keeping accuracy close to AR SFT. With block size four, Lafa exceeds DeepSeek-MTP in both accuracy and TPF; with block size eight, it matches the accuracy of MARS with block size four at about 1.5 its TPF. At 8B, Lafa achieves similar accuracy and TPF to Efficient-DLM despite using at least 18 fewer training tokens. Across scales, Lafa achieves approximately 2.55 TPF while remaining close to or above AR SFT accuracy. Wall-clock throughput. Since forward-pass costs differ across methods, we also measure end-to-end throughput at 78B scales on single H100 GPU with batch size one, using each methods native decoder. Figure 8 reports accuracy and throughput in tokens per second (TPS), averaged over IFEval, GSM8K, and HumanEval (settings and perbenchmark results in Appendix C.2). With block size sixteen, Lafa 7B achieves 2.54 the throughput of 7B AR SFT at comparable average accuracy. With block size four, it is about twice as fast while also more accurate on average. DeepSeek-MTP and MARS match or exceed AR SFT accuracy but achieve at most 1.4 its throughput. Diffusion baselines fall below 7B AR SFT accuracy, faster settings showing larger losses. Thus, while flow decoding requires multiple integration steps to reach AR quality (Section 3.1), verifying one-step flow drafts enables substantially faster generation at comparable quality. Figure 8: Accuracy vs. end-to-end throughput measured in tokens per second (TPS) at 78B scales, averaged over IFEval, GSM8K, and HumanEval. Accepting drafts by confidence thresholding instead of AR verification trades accuracy for speed. We therefore use self-speculation as our default fast decoding mode and report confidence decoding results in Appendix C.3.

sections.title: 3.4 Ablations
sections.content: We ablate the main training and inference choices in Section 2 using flow decoding to assess their effect on the learned flow. All comparisons use 0.5B models with block size four and 32 Euler integration steps  (Table 3)  . For training, block-bidirectional attention and learned tokenwise time both improve accuracy over their causal and synchronous counterparts. Learning embedding directions while fixing their norms outperforms both frozen embeddings and unconstrained updates. Combining denoising cross entropy and embedding squared error improves accuracy over either objective alone. Adding prefix AR loss improves flow accuracy further, showing that retaining AR capabilities need not compromise flow generation. For inference, both self-conditioning and prefix guidance improve accuracy. Self-conditioning provides the larger gain while requiring no additional model evaluations during decoding. sections.title: 4 Related work
sections.content: In this section, we review existing representative approaches for parallel language modeling. Block-autoregressive language models. Block-autoregressive models reduce sequential generation by producing blocks of tokens conditioned on preceding blocks. Approaches to parallel block generation include multi-token prediction (MTP) heads or modules [6, 8], and predictors that take masked or noisy blocks as input [23, 33, 46]. Many parallel decoders predict tokens independently within an update, which can degrade quality when many tokens are committed at once [13]. Some methods mitigate this through AR verification or confidence-based acceptance of draft prefix [8, 33, 41]. Some recent methods learn deterministic noise-to-token maps that can capture joint dependencies without independent output sampling [47, 57]. Discrete diffusion language models. Discrete diffusion models generate text by reversing discrete corruption process, such as masking or random token replacement, through iterative denoising [5861]. As with other parallel decoders, independent sampling within each update can limit quality in few-step generation [62, 63]. These models have been scaled to billions of parameters [11, 20, 21, 45], with generation performed over entire sequences or individual blocks. Block diffusion [23] combines iterative denoising within each block with autoregressive generation and prefix caching across blocks. Continuous diffusion and flow language models. Continuous diffusion and flow models generate text through noisy continuous representations, including token embeddings, simplex representations, and binary encodings [12, 18, 28, 37, 6467]. Continuous flows transport joint sequence representations and admit flow maps that can be learned for few-step generation [13, 38]. Recent work has demonstrated competitive generation quality and improved few-step decoding [1317, 36, 68], while few recent efforts have explored billion-parameter scales [6972]. Related approaches also study autoregression and diffusion over autoencoded continuous representations [7376]. Realizing the benefits of continuous flows at large and practical scale calls for data-efficient training and fast inference. Lafa addresses both by aligning blockwise asynchronous flows with the causal structure of pretrained AR models. This enables efficient adaptation and prefix caching, while retained AR prediction supports self-speculative generation.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Lafa, blockwise flow language model scaled to 8B parameters by adapting pretrained AR models with fewer than 30B training tokens. Lafa combines causal generation across blocks with learned asynchronous flows within each block, preserving prefix caching while enabling parallel generation. With sufficient integration steps, flow decoding approaches or surpasses AR SFT accuracy, and flow map distillation improves few-step generation. Joint training also improves AR accuracy over matched AR SFT. This retained AR predictor verifies one-step flow drafts within the same model, enabling self-speculative decoding. With this approach, Lafa 7B achieves 2.54 the throughput of the 7B AR SFT baseline at comparable average accuracy. These results demonstrate practical path to scaling continuous flows for language modeling through data-efficient AR adaptation. Improving flow map distillation, particularly its incorporation of self-conditioning and prefix guidance, remains promising direction for further accelerating flow generation.
